questions.q: What are the four stages of the project's 2-qubit circuit, in order?
options: Measure, encode, entangle, ansatz
Encode (RY per feature), trainable ansatz (RY per qubit), entangle (CNOT), measure <Z> on qubit 1
Only two stages: encode and measure, with no trainable ansatz at all
Entangle, measure, encode, ansatz
questions.explain: The circuit assembles angle encoding (Lesson 10), a trainable ansatz (Lesson 6), an entangling CNOT, and a final Z measurement on qubit 1 (Lesson 12's classifier structure).

questions.q: With the untrained ansatz (theta1=theta2=0.5), the Setosa sample (true label 0) produces p approximately 0.8029. What does this indicate?
options: The untrained circuit is confidently WRONG for this sample, which is expected and fine for an untuned random starting point
This is the correct prediction for Setosa, since Setosa is actually labeled 1
This proves the circuit architecture is fundamentally broken
The circuit is already perfectly trained and needs no further updates
questions.explain: p approximately 0.80 for a true label of 0 means the untrained model confidently predicts the wrong class -- exactly what's expected from an arbitrary, untuned starting point, analogous to a classical network's random initialization.

questions.q: After one parameter-shift gradient step updating only theta1 using the Setosa sample, what happens to the Setosa sample's loss?
options: It drops to exactly zero, indicating perfect classification
It increases, revealing a bug in the gradient computation
It drops substantially, from approximately 1.6241 to approximately 0.5483, confirming the update genuinely helped
It stays exactly the same since only one parameter was updated
questions.explain: Recomputing the forward pass with the updated theta1 shows the loss drop from about 1.6241 to about 0.5483 -- a large, verified improvement confirming the parameter-shift gradient and update were computed correctly.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say this single verified gradient step does NOT yet constitute a trained classifier?
options: A real training run needs many iterations across the entire training set, updating all parameters together, until loss stabilizes across the whole dataset, plus a held-out test set to check generalization
Because parameter-shift gradients are mathematically invalid for multi-qubit circuits
Because the circuit would need at least 50 qubits to be considered trained
Because the Setosa and Versicolor samples used real Iris measurements, which cannot be used for training
questions.explain: One gradient step using one sample and one parameter only verifies the mechanism works -- genuine training requires iterating over the full dataset, updating every parameter together, and checking generalization on held-out data, which Lesson 25 addresses.

questions.q: Why might updating theta1 using only the Versicolor sample's gradient push theta1 in a different direction than the Setosa sample's gradient did?
options: Gradient direction is determined solely by the learning rate, not by the sample's label or features
Versicolor and Setosa always produce identical gradients regardless of their labels

Each sample has a different true label and different encoded feature values, so each one's loss landscape with respect to theta1 can point in a different direction -- which is exactly why a real training loop must account for every sample, not just one, before drawing conclusions
The parameter-shift rule only works for one specific sample per circuit, never multiple
questions.explain: Different samples (different features, different true labels) can push a shared parameter in different directions -- this is exactly why real training averages or iterates over the whole dataset rather than updating based on a single sample's gradient alone.
